docs.title: 7. Summary
docs.text:
The majority of client requirements for the Intermediate phase were already established during the Sprint 1 client meetings. As a result, the team required only limited follow-up interaction during this phase.

Rather than creating artificial or unnecessary meetings, the team continued development using the requirements and architectural decisions previously confirmed by the client. Where clarification was required, questions were raised through the team's existing WhatsApp communication channel.

This approach allowed the team to continue development while maintaining a record of the decisions that informed the implementation.

The project documentation was also made accessible online through the deployed MkDocs site, with the documentation link included in the project README.

docs.title: Feature Audit — September 2026
docs.text: Repository: coms3011a-logbook-digital-logbook Branch: Dineo at 7d0af0a, level with origin/main Date: 2026-09-20 Method: code-level verification against the working tree, both test suites run on the development machine, and a manual walkthrough against local dev servers (backend on 3000, Vite on 5173) signed in as the project owner. Every verdict was reached by reading the file or exercising the feature named beside it.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text: This audit establishes what works before the UI transformation begins, so a regression introduced later can be told apart from a defect that was already there. It also re-checks the ten bugs and eight features recorded in .gitea/issues/.

docs.title: 2. Test suites
docs.text:
Both suites pass in full. Run on the development machine on 2026-09-20; they cannot be run from the audit environment, because the organisation's egress policy blocks registry.npmjs.org and TCP 5432 to the Neon host, and the installed node_modules are Windows binaries.

Suite Files Tests Result apps/backend 7 130 130 passed, 0 failed (94.13s) apps/frontend 8 65 65 passed, 0 failed (12.25s)

The known flaky TOTP timing test did not fail on this run. The previously recorded expectation of "100 backend tests" is out of date; the suite has grown to 130.

Four warnings are worth acting on even though nothing failed. The pg driver reports that sslmode=require in the Neon connection string is currently treated as verify-full and will adopt weaker libpq semantics in pg v9 — a one-word change to the connection string settles it before that lands. A client.query() when the client is already executing a query deprecation fires across several suites. The frontend suites emit React act(...) warnings in EntryForm, LoginPage and RegisterPage, meaning those assertions race their state updates. And jsdom cannot implement getContext(), so every canvas render bails — the chart components are effectively untested, which matters before Phase B restyles them.

docs.title: 3. BUG-011 — No ownership checks on the entry and statistics APIs
docs.text:
Severity: High (broken access control). Component: apps/backend/src/controllers/entry.controller.ts, apps/backend/src/controllers/stats.controller.ts.

getEntries (entry.controller.ts:74) queries where: { projectId } with no userId term. createEntry (:126) resolves the project with findUnique({ where: { id: projectId } }) alone. deleteEntry (:263) and updateEntryStatus (:96) perform no ownership check at all. updateEntry (:177) reads project.userId but uses it only to resolve tag ownership, never comparing it to req.userId. All five are typed req: Request, not AuthenticatedRequest.

The same omission appears in stats.controller.ts: groupStats (:6) and timelineStats (:91) are typed req: Request, so they cannot read req.userId even in principle, and their entryField lookups are scoped by projectId only.

The routes are wrapped in requireAuth (entry.routes.ts:14-20), but that middleware establishes only that the caller holds a valid JWT, not that the caller owns the resource named in the path. Any authenticated account can therefore read, modify, delete and aggregate another account's entries given an ID, and project IDs appear in the address bar on /projects/:id.

Why it was not previously recorded: the backlog was assembled from a code scan for TODOs and security patterns, from AUTHENTICATION.md's documented limitations, and from the commit history. An authorisation check that is simply absent leaves no pattern to scan for and no comment to read. project.controller.ts and entryField.controller.ts both scope correctly by userId, so the codebase looks consistent until these two files are compared against them directly.

docs.title: 4. BUG-012 — A blank numeric field breaks every aggregation and leaks the database error
docs.text:
Severity: High. Component: apps/frontend/src/lib/utils.ts, apps/backend/src/utils/entryValues.ts, apps/backend/src/controllers/stats.controller.ts.

Reproduced end to end during the walkthrough. The chain is five steps, each individually defensible:

  1. defaultValuesForFields (frontend/src/lib/utils.ts:74-86) seeds every field the user has not touched, and its else branch at :83 assigns "" — so an untouched NUMBER field is submitted as an empty string.
  2. checkValueShape (backend/src/utils/entryValues.ts:18) returns null for any empty value before reaching the NUMBER branch, so "" passes validation without a type check.
  3. createEntry (backend/src/controllers/entry.controller.ts:158-161) writes the value through String(value ?? ""), storing an EntryValue row whose value is the empty string.
  4. groupStats (backend/src/controllers/stats.controller.ts:40) builds its metric expression by casting (mv.value)::numeric with no guard, and timelineStats (:134) does the same for SUM. Postgres raises 22P02 invalid input syntax for type numeric: "" and the endpoint returns 500.
  5. flattenValues (backend/src/controllers/entry.controller.ts:23) renders a stored "" as Number(ev.value) || 0, i.e. 0, so the entry list shows a tidy "Hours: 0" and nothing looks wrong until the statistics page is opened.

Sum, average, min and max on that field are all dead until the row is corrected. Verified live: with one entry holding Hours = 3 and one holding "", all three of avg, min and sum returned HTTP 500.

There is a second defect inside the first. StatsPage.tsx:145 and :170 render err?.response?.data?.error verbatim, and the backend's catch block passes error.message through unchanged, so the user is shown the literal text Invalid prisma.$queryRawUnsafe() invocation: Raw query failed. Code: 22P02. Message: invalid input syntax for type numeric: "" inside a red panel. An internal database error reaches the interface.

Worth noting when fixing: utils/entryFormat.ts:53-69 carries a long comment explaining, correctly, that backfillNewField refuses to fabricate a 0 for pre-existing entries because doing so "would silently drag the average down and force the min to 0". The entry form then does exactly that for every newly created entry. Whichever way this is fixed — storing nothing for an untouched field, or guarding the cast in SQL — the two halves should end up agreeing.

Why it was not previously recorded: it needs three files to be read together, and the symptom is invisible in the entry list because step 5 masks it as a clean 0. The backend tests cover numeric validation (entryValidation.test.ts asserts a non-numeric value is rejected) but no test creates an entry that simply leaves a NUMBER field alone and then aggregates over it.

docs.title: 5. BUG-013 — Duplicate React keys in the project field editor
docs.text:
Severity: Medium. Component: apps/frontend/src/pages/ProjectsPage.tsx.

addField (:139) creates each new row with id: `new-${Date.now()}`, and the rows are rendered with key={field.id} (:383). Two "+ Add Field" clicks landing in the same millisecond therefore produce two rows with an identical key. React's reconciliation is undefined in that case — it may duplicate or omit rows.

Reproduced: rapid repeated clicking on "+ Add Field" produced fifteen rows from nine clicks, with the console logging Encountered two children with the same key, new-1789920217358. The same ids double as identity for removal (:148 tests id.startsWith("new-")), so a collision affects deletion as well as rendering.

A counter, crypto.randomUUID(), or index-free stable ids would all fix it.

Why it was not previously recorded: it only surfaces under fast repeated clicks, which a manual tester adding fields one at a time will never trigger, and the frontend suite has no test for the field editor.

docs.title: 6. BUG-014 — Project and entry lists fan out one request per project and block on all of them
docs.text:
Severity: Medium (performance). Component: apps/frontend/src/pages/ProjectsPage.tsx, and the same shape in DashboardPage.tsx and EntriesPage.tsx.

loadProjects (ProjectsPage.tsx:63-93) sets loading true, awaits fetchProjects(), then awaits a Promise.all over every returned project calling fetchProjectTimeSummary(p.id), and only clears loading in the finally once all of them have resolved. The list therefore cannot render until the slowest per-project request completes, and the number of requests grows linearly with the number of projects. DashboardPage.tsx:161 and EntriesPage.tsx:63 fan out fetchEntries(p.id) per project in the same way.

Observed: against a local dev server with three projects, the projects page held its "Loading projects…" state for roughly eleven seconds. Each round trip goes to Neon in us-east-2, so the per-request latency is what makes an N+1 expensive here.

Correction to an earlier draft of this audit. An earlier note claimed the app issues duplicated requests — /api/projects four times and /api/tags twice in a single page load. That claim does not survive checking. main.tsx wraps the app in <React.StrictMode>, and React double-invokes effects in development only. The doubling is StrictMode behaving as designed and does not occur in a production build. The N+1 fan-out and the blocking loading state above are real in both; the duplication is not a defect and should not be reported as one.

Why it was not previously recorded: the backlog was built from static inspection, and an N+1 is only visible once the number of projects and the database round-trip latency are both considered.

docs.title: 7. BUG-015 — No delete-project endpoint
docs.text:
Severity: Low. Component: apps/backend/src/routes/project.routes.ts.

The router defines POST /projects, GET /projects, GET /projects/:id, GET /projects/:id/time-summary, PUT /projects/:id and PATCH /projects/:id/status (:14-19). There is no delete route, and deleteProject does not exist anywhere in the backend or the frontend. Verified live: DELETE /api/projects/:id returns 404.

This is defensible against the specification, which asks only that projects be "created, described, and archived once they are finished", and the archive flow works correctly. It is recorded because the interface offers no way to remove a project created by mistake, and because the walkthrough's own test project could not be cleaned up afterwards — it had to be archived instead.

Why it was not previously recorded: a missing route leaves nothing to scan for, and archiving covers the specification's stated requirement, so nothing in the documentation points at the gap.

docs.title: 8. Manual walkthrough
docs.text:
A project named AUDIT TEST 2026-09 was created with all nine field types, exercised, and archived at the end.

Area Verdict Notes Login, session, protected routes Works Dashboard render Works Greeting, three stat cards, deadlines panel, activity chart, current projects, tags, recent entries Project create with tags, edit, archive, unarchive Works Entries still addable to an archived project Works Confirmed by API — archiving is a filter, not a lock, as intended Entry format: eight of nine types Works TEXT, NUMBER, DATE, BOOLEAN, TAGS, CHECKLIST, LINK, REFERENCE all created and round-tripped correctly COMPUTED at project-creation time Broken See below COMPUTED added to an existing project Works The edit modal exposes "Formula ID" next to each numeric field, and the formula evaluates Computed backfill onto existing entries Works An entry with Hours = 3 picked up Double hours = 6 when the computed field was added afterwards Format versions immutable Works The entry stayed pinned to format version 8 after two later format changes Entry create, tags, due date, backdating Works Values stored and rendered correctly, including checklist items and the reference Statistics — time per project, group-by, plot over time Works, except BUG-012 Dark mode Partly broken See §9 Search, saved filters, calendar, board, open work Present, not individually exercised Code verified; runtime pass deferred Offline queue, export/import Present, not exercised Deferred Session-expiry redirect Verified by code and unit test only Not exercised live, to avoid disturbing the signed-in session

COMPUTED at creation time. The create-project modal offers "Computed number" as a field type and a formula box whose placeholder is Formula, e.g. {numeric-field-id} * 2. At that moment no field has an ID yet, so there is no valid formula a user could type. Submitting sends the other fields successfully and the computed one returns 400, leaving a project with eight of its nine fields. The type should not be offered until the project exists, or the modal should accept a field reference by name and resolve it server-side.

Reference fields. The REFERENCE picker lists other projects only. The specification asks for "links from one entry to another, references between projects" — entry-to-entry references are not implemented.

Computed fields in the entry form render as read-only text reading Calculated automatically: {6256bbd2-…} * 2. The user is shown a raw UUID where a field name belongs.

docs.title: 9. Theming
docs.text:
Dark mode is implemented in index.css as thirteen [data-theme="dark"] overrides covering bg-white, bg-slate-50/100, border-slate-100/200, the text-slate-400 through text-slate-900 range, one hover state and the form controls. Nothing else is themed.

Confirmed visually: with dark mode on, the statistics error panel renders as a near-white bg-red-50 box with text-red-600 text on the dark page. The same applies to every surface built from bg-red-50 (eighteen uses), border-red-200 (sixteen), bg-blue-50 (twelve), bg-emerald-50 (nine) and bg-amber-50 (four) — error panels, deadline cards, stat tiles and tag chips all stay light.

The accent colour is split. bg-blue-600 and its relatives appear about seventy times across pages/ and components/, while text-cyan-600, text-cyan-700 and text-cyan-400 appear fourteen times, concentrated in the sidebar and the statistics page. The day/week/month toggle on the statistics page is visibly cyan while every other primary control is blue.

Extending the override set and consolidating on one accent are prerequisites for Phase B, not polish to be added afterwards.

docs.title: 10. Performance baseline
docs.text:
Measured from the committed build in apps/frontend/dist/assets, dated 2026-09-20 14:54 UTC:

Asset Bytes Approx. index-C9NAvquY.js 533,540 521 KB (~150 KB gzipped) index-DVfC3cdS.css 45,134 44 KB

Every later bundle measurement is compared against these two numbers. The runtime cost described in BUG-014 is the more pressing half of the client's complaint that the app is slow, and it is independent of bundle size.

Separately, components/Sidebar.tsx writes a radial-gradient into an inline style on every mouse move (:100-106) and renders five particle spans (:234-240), which index.css drives through five infinite keyframe animations plus a sixth on the avatar ring (:104-206). Six permanently running animations sit behind every page. prefers-reduced-motion appears nowhere in the frontend, so none of this can be turned off by a viewer who asks for less motion — a live failure against FEAT-006 before any Phase B motion is added.

docs.title: 11. The seven documented gaps, re-checked
docs.text:
Gap 1 — EntryForm renders only four of nine field types. Confirmed, and wider than recorded. components/EntryForm.tsx handles TEXT, NUMBER, DATE and BOOLEAN only. It also has no entryDate input and does not carry tags, so backdating and tagging exist solely inside the bespoke modal in ProjectDetailPage, which does render all nine.

Gap 2 — no global quick entry. Confirmed. AppLayout.tsx has no New Entry control and the sidebar offers none. A search of the whole frontend for metaKey or ctrlKey returns one match: the Ctrl+Enter submit inside EntryForm. There is no Ctrl/Cmd+N and no command palette.

Gap 3 — decorative sidebar effects. Confirmed, with the cost described in §10.

Gap 4 — dashboard structure. Partly confirmed. The page has the greeting, stat cards, deadlines, activity, current projects, tags and recent entries. It lacks a New Entry action, and ProjectCard.tsx makes no reference to fields, so there are no format summaries.

Gap 5 — no field builder on Project Detail. Confirmed. The page renders an "Entry Format" section listing fields read-only with a format-history link. None of createEntryField, updateEntryField or deleteEntryField is called from it; all three live in ProjectsPage's edit modal.

Gap 6 — due dates rely on colour. Largely refuted. EntryCard renders a textual "Overdue" badge, and DeadlineReminders and OpenWorkPage pair labels with icons. The real defect is duplication: there is no shared DueDateBadge, so each surface derives and renders urgency independently.

Gap 7 — statistics incomplete. Largely refuted. The statistics page offers a project selector, a metric field with all five operations, group-by over any non-computed field, and a timeline with day/week/month buckets plotting entry counts or a numeric total. Two gaps remain. The timeline requires the project to have a user-defined DATE field, so a project without one cannot be plotted at all even though every entry carries entryDate. And the metric selector lists only NUMBER and COMPUTED fields, so although the backend accepts count over TEXT, TAGS and BOOLEAN, counting entries grouped by a text field is unreachable from the interface.

docs.title: 13. Repository hygiene
docs.text:
The working tree is clean, but only when git is told core.autocrlf=true. Git for Windows sets that in its system configuration; environments that do not, including any Linux or CI checkout, see all 204 tracked files as modified. git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol is empty, confirming the difference is entirely line endings. A .gitattributes containing * text=auto eol=lf would settle it permanently.

prisma/migrations/ holds only 20260908000000_entry_format_versions and 20260920000000_add_tags. There is no baseline migration for the core eleven-model schema, so a fresh environment brought up with prisma migrate deploy would not arrive at the current schema. The tags migration exists locally; whether it has been applied to the production Neon database — an open item from the 2026-09-18 client meeting — could not be checked, as that database is unreachable from the audit environment.

The MkDocs build output in site/ is committed to the repository and accounts for most of the line-ending churn above.

docs.title: 14. Recommended sequence
docs.text:
Phase C should lead with BUG-011 and BUG-012, then BUG-002 and BUG-003. BUG-011 and BUG-012 both need no misconfiguration to trigger — one is exploitable by any signed-in account, the other by any user who leaves a number blank — while BUG-002 requires a deployment mistake. The remainder of the recorded order stands.

Phase B should treat four items as prerequisites rather than polish: extending the dark-mode override set before any new coloured surface is introduced, adding a prefers-reduced-motion guard before any motion is added, removing the six always-on sidebar animations, and fixing the N+1 in BUG-014. Together these are the cheapest honest answer to the client's complaint about speed, and none of them depends on any of the 3D work.

docs.title: 15. Not yet covered
docs.text: Search and saved filters, the calendar and board views, open work, the offline queue and sync, JSON and CSV export and import, and the live session-expiry redirect were verified by reading their code but not exercised in the browser. The live deployment was not probed. These are the remaining items for a second walkthrough.

docs.title: 1.1 Methodology Used
docs.text:
We use a Kanban-based methodology with individual functional-area ownership rather than a traditional fixed-length Scrum sprint model.

The project is organised into functional areas, with user stories assigned to team members according to the relationships and dependencies between features.

For Sprint 1 – Core Logbook, the user stories were distributed as follows:

Team Member User Stories Functional Area Person 1 US00.1, US00.2, US00.3, US00.4 Authentication & Account Management Person 2 US01, US05 Project Management Person 3 US02, US03 Entry Structure & Entry Creation Person 4 US04, US06 Time Tracking & Entry Browsing

Work flows through a single shared Kanban board with columns:

Backlog → To Do → In Progress → Done

Each team member manages the flow of their assigned stories while coordinating with other members when cross-area dependencies arise.

For the Intermediate phase, work was divided into four functional areas:

Team Member User Stories Functional Area Person 1 US07, US08, US09, US10 Entry Formats & Fields Person 2 US11, US12, US13 Statistics & Views Person 3 US14, US15 Offline & Data Person 4 Integration & Testing Cross-feature Integration

For Sprint 3 – Advanced Logbook, work was again divided into four functional areas:

Team Member User Stories Functional Area Member 1 US22, US23, US24 Custom Statistics & Expressions Member 2 US25, US26, US27, US28 Personal Dashboard & Automation Member 3 US29, US30, US31, US32 Versioning & Record History Member 4 US33, US34, US35, US36, US37 Advanced Search & Performance

docs.title: 1.2 Reasoning & Motivation
docs.text:
• Why Kanban instead of Scrum: The project contains features with clear functional dependencies rather than work that must always be completed simultaneously within a fixed sprint. Kanban allows team members to progress their assigned functionality while making dependencies visible.

The core dependency chain established during Sprint 1 was:

Authentication → Projects → Entry Formats → Entries → Time Tracking / Browsing

The Intermediate phase builds on this foundation by extending entry formats and adding functionality that operates across existing logbook data:

Entry Formats → Rich Fields / Computed Fields → Statistics / Views → Offline / Data Portability

Sprint 3 operates on data whose shape the platform does not know in advance, so each area builds on the custom-field and entry model from the earlier phases. Its dependency chains were:

Custom Fields → Custom Expressions → Saved Statistics → Dashboard Panels → Dashboard Persistence

Entries → Version History → Historical Viewing → Restore Previous Version

Entries & Due Dates → Automation Rules / Recurring Entries → Automatic Reminders → Device Notifications

Custom Fields → Structured Search → Combined Filters → Result Ranking

Saved statistics (US23) had to exist before they could be offered as dashboard panels (US25), and version history (US29) had to record every change before a past state could be viewed (US30) or restored (US31). Archiving (US32) and long-term query performance (US33) apply across all of the above.

  • Functional Ownership: Related stories are assigned to the same developer where possible. For example, US07–US10 are closely related because they all extend the entry-format system, and US29–US31 all depend on the same version-history records. Keeping these stories together allows one developer to maintain consistency between related features.

  • Handling Cross-Area Dependencies: We use a status:blocked-on-dependency label. A story waiting on an upstream dependency remains in Backlog with this label. Once the required contract, schema, or functionality is available, the label is removed and the issue can move to To Do.

docs.title: Intermediate Phase
docs.text:
The Intermediate user stories US07–US15 have been completed.

The Intermediate phase extended the Basic Digital Logbook with:

  • Richer field types.
  • Modification of existing entry formats.
  • Preservation of previous entry-format versions.
  • Computed fields.
  • Statistics based on custom fields.
  • Alternative entry views.
  • Unfinished-work and due-date tracking.
  • Offline entry capture and synchronisation.
  • Logbook data export and import.

docs.title: Sprint 3 – Advanced Logbook
docs.text:
Status on the Sprint 3 board:

Area Stories Status Custom Statistics & Expressions US22, US23, US24 Done Personal Dashboard & Automation US25, US26, US27, US28 Done Versioning & Record History US29, US30, US31 Done Versioning & Record History US32 In Progress Advanced Search & Performance US33 Done Advanced Search & Performance US34, US35, US36, US37 Backlog

Eleven of the sixteen stories are done. The completed stories added:

  • Custom expressions over an owner's own entries, saved as statistics alongside the built-in ones.
  • Automation rules evaluated when an entry is created or saved, which can add or remove tags and set status.
  • A personal dashboard whose panels, including saved statistics, are chosen, arranged, and stored on the server.
  • Recurring entries generated from a stored template on a daily, weekly, or monthly pattern.
  • Automatic reminders for upcoming and overdue due dates, stalled entries, and a daily logging reminder, delivered as web push notifications when the logbook is closed.
  • A version history for every entry, a view of an entry as it stood on a given date, and restoring an earlier version.
  • Faster queries on a long record: database indexes on the common lookup columns, a paginated Entries page, and a single request for open work instead of one per project.

docs.title: 3.1 Sprint 1 – What Went Well
docs.text:
• Vertical slice delivery: All 10 core user stories from authentication through time tracking and entry browsing were implemented as end-to-end vertical slices covering the database, API, and UI.

  • Shared types package: Extracting types into @logbook/shared eliminated duplication and helped identify type mismatches between the frontend and backend early.

  • Integration testing: 27 Vitest tests running against the Neon database provided confidence that API endpoints worked correctly, including edge cases such as duplicate names, missing resources, and invalid input. The suite has since grown to 33 backend and 24 frontend test files.

  • Prisma ORM adoption: Migrating from raw SQL to Prisma simplified database access and provided type-safe queries.

  • Kanban workflow: The dependency-chain model worked well with functional ownership and made dependencies between areas visible to the team.

docs.title: 3.2 Intermediate Phase – What Went Well
docs.text:
• Feature ownership: Grouping related Intermediate stories by functional area helped maintain consistency between related features.

  • Extension of the existing system: The Intermediate features were developed on top of the Sprint 1 foundation rather than requiring a separate system.

  • Integration and testing: Dedicated integration work helped identify issues occurring between independently developed features and ensured that the new functionality continued to work with existing features.

  • Flexible entry model: Extending the entry-format system with richer fields and computed values moved the project closer to the specification's requirement for customisable logbook entries.

docs.title: 3.3 Sprint 3 – What Went Well
docs.text:
• Building on stored history: Because every save writes a version record, later features could rely on it. Automation rules record what they changed as their own version, so an automatic change can be seen and undone like a manual one.

  • Safe automation: Automation rules run only after an entry has been saved, cannot trigger themselves or each other, and skip a broken rule rather than failing the save, so a misconfigured rule never costs the user their entry.

  • Server-side persistence: Saving the dashboard layout on the server rather than in the browser means a student sees the same dashboard on every device.

docs.title: 3.4 What Could Be Improved
docs.text:
• Frontend error handling: The frontend uses basic error banners for API failures. A proper toast notification system would improve the user experience. Some failures are also reported misleadingly: when the backend cannot be reached, the login page reports "Invalid email or password."

  • Test isolation: Integration tests run against the live database without transaction rollback. Tests create and clean up data, but parallel test runs could potentially conflict.

  • Documentation gaps: Some documentation was written towards the end of development rather than incrementally. Future work should update documentation alongside implementation.

  • Cross-feature integration: As more Intermediate features were introduced, dependencies between features became more complex. Earlier integration of completed components would reduce the risk of discovering compatibility issues near the end of development.

  • Testing features that depend on deployment: Push notifications only work in a production build, and the hosted backend sleeps when idle on Render's free tier. Features like these need a deployed test environment, not only local development.

docs.title: 4. Remaining Improvements
docs.text:
Several improvements identified from client feedback after the Intermediate phase have since been delivered:

  • Unit tests now sit alongside integration tests for complex business logic, such as the expression evaluator and automation-rule conditions.
  • Google Calendar integration.
  • A live stopwatch in entry creation and editing.
  • Per-project cumulative time on the Project Detail page.
  • Deadline reminders with device notifications (US28).

Improvements that remain useful for further development:

  1. Add frontend toast notifications for API errors, and distinguish "server unreachable" from "wrong credentials".
  2. Improve the visual presentation of overdue entries.

These items are treated as future improvements rather than incomplete user stories.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Tool Version Notes Node.js v22+ Use nvm (recommended) npm v10+ Ships with Node.js nvm latest Optional, manages Node versions PostgreSQL — Hosted on Neon — no local install needed

docs.title: 1. Clone the repository
docs.text:
git clone https://sdp.ms.wits.ac.za/no-boys-just-bugs/coms3011a-logbook-digital-logbook.git
cd coms3011a-logbook-digital-logbook

docs.title: 2. Set the Node version
docs.text: nvm use

docs.title: 3. Install dependencies
docs.text:
From the repository root (installs all workspace packages):

npm install

Then build the shared package once:

npm run build --workspace=packages/shared

@logbook/shared ships compiled JavaScript and declarations rather than TypeScript source, and the backend resolves it through packages/shared/dist. Until it is built, the backend fails to start with Cannot find module '…/node_modules/@logbook/shared/dist/index.js'. Re-run it after changing anything in packages/shared/src, or the backend keeps using the old build. (The frontend reads packages/shared/src directly through an alias in vite.config.ts, so it does not need the build.)

docs.title: 4. Configure environment variables
docs.text:
Create apps/backend/.env from the example file:

cp apps/backend/.env.example apps/backend/.env

Then edit apps/backend/.env. The example is a template, not working values: delete or blank every placeholder you are not replacing with a real value. A leftover placeholder such as RESEND_API_KEY=re_xxxxxxxxxxxxx makes the backend believe email is configured, so new accounts are no longer auto-verified and cannot sign in.

Required for local development:

Variable Purpose DATABASE_URL Neon connection string (Neon dashboard → Connection Details). Contains the database password. PORT Backend port, normally 3000 (the Vite proxy expects it). APP_URL Frontend URL, http://localhost:5173 locally. Used in email links and the Google Calendar redirect. JWT_SECRET Signs login tokens. Optional locally, but without it the backend generates a new secret on every start, so every restart signs you out. Required in production, where the server refuses to start without it.

Generate any secret in this guide with:

node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(48).toString('hex'))"

Optional, per feature: leave these unset and the feature is simply off.

Variable(s) Feature Without it RESEND_API_KEY, RESEND_FROM Email via Resend (recommended) Accounts are auto-verified; links are logged to the backend console GMAIL_USER, GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD Email via Gmail SMTP (used only when Resend is not set) As above TWO_FACTOR_ENCRYPTION_KEY Encrypts 2FA secrets Enabling 2FA returns 503. Never change it once set: existing 2FA users would be locked out GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID, GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET, GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI, GOOGLE_TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY Google Calendar sync The Calendar page reports that Google Calendar is not configured VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY, VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY (and optionally VAPID_SUBJECT) Push notifications for reminders (see Push notifications) Reminders stay in-app only; the backend logs VAPID keys not set on start RATE_LIMIT_*, RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED, TRUST_PROXY_HOPS Rate-limit tuning Sensible defaults apply; see the comments in .env.example

Warning: Never commit .env files with real credentials to the repository, and never paste real connection strings or keys into documentation — the docs site is publicly accessible. .env is already listed in .gitignore.

docs.title: 5. Set up the database schema
docs.text:
The backend uses Prisma 7 with a prisma.config.ts file that reads the DATABASE_URL from your .env. All Prisma commands must be run from inside the apps/backend/ directory:

cd apps/backend
npx prisma generate
npx prisma migrate deploy

The migration history was squashed on 2026-09-27 into a baseline, prisma/migrations/0_init, which creates the core schema (eighteen tables, enums, unique indexes and foreign keys) on an empty database. Dated migrations after it add the rest — push subscriptions, dashboard layouts, and unique entry-field names — for twenty tables in all. npx prisma migrate deploy applies them in order, so it bootstraps a fresh Neon project end-to-end; there is no need for prisma db push, and new schema changes should arrive as dated migrations (npx prisma migrate dev --name <change>).

docs.title: 6. Run development servers
docs.text:
You need both servers running simultaneously:

Terminal 1 — Backend (Express API on port 3000):

npm run dev --workspace=backend

Terminal 2 — Frontend (Vite dev server on port 5173):

npm run dev --workspace=frontend

The frontend proxies /api/* requests to http://localhost:3000 via the Vite config.

Open http://localhost:5173 in your browser to use the app.

Note: Both servers must be running. Without the backend, the Vite terminal logs http proxy error: /api/… ECONNREFUSED and every request fails — see Troubleshooting.

When the backend starts you will see a SECURITY WARNING from pg about SSL modes. It is harmless; changing sslmode=require to sslmode=verify-full in DATABASE_URL silences it without changing behaviour.

docs.title: Code Quality & Linting
docs.text:
The frontend uses oxlint for fast linting:

npm run lint --workspace=frontend

The backend uses TypeScript's built-in type checker. Run it before committing:

npm run typecheck --workspace=backend

Note: The backend does not have a separate lint script. The root-level npm run lint command uses --if-present, so it will skip the backend gracefully.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Both apps use Vitest.

  • Backend (apps/backend/src/__tests__/): integration tests using Supertest, one file per area (auth, entries, statistics, reminders, push, automation rules and so on). They run against the database in apps/backend/.env, so that file must be set up first.
  • Frontend (apps/frontend/src/**/__tests__/): component, page and library tests using Testing Library in jsdom. They mock the API and need no backend.
# Run all tests
npm run test --workspace=backend
npm run test --workspace=frontend

# Run tests in watch mode
npm run test:watch --workspace=backend

docs.title: Shared Types Package
docs.text:
The @logbook/shared package (packages/shared/) contains TypeScript interfaces, Zod validation schemas, and types shared between frontend and backend. It is linked via npm workspaces ("@logbook/shared": "*").

After modifying shared types: 1. Rebuild the package: npm run build --workspace=packages/shared 2. Restart both dev servers

After changing apps/backend/prisma/schema.prisma, regenerate the Prisma client with npx prisma generate from apps/backend/.

docs.title: Authentication & Email
docs.text:
The app uses JWT-based authentication with email verification and optional two-factor authentication (2FA):

  • Registration creates a user with an unverified email
  • Email verification — a verification link is sent by email (if configured)
  • Login is blocked until the email is verified
  • Password reset — reset link sent via email
  • Two-factor authentication (2FA) — TOTP-based 2FA using otplib, with recovery codes. Users can enable/disable 2FA in Settings. When enabled, a QR code is generated for authenticator app setup. Requires TWO_FACTOR_ENCRYPTION_KEY.

Dev mode (no email provider): accounts are automatically verified so you can develop without email setup. The verification link is logged to the backend console.

Real email: set RESEND_API_KEY and RESEND_FROM (recommended), or GMAIL_USER and GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD. If both are set, Resend is used.

docs.title: Push notifications
docs.text:
Reminders can notify a device even when the logbook is closed, using web push.

  1. Generate a key pair once: npx web-push generate-vapid-keys.
  2. Put the pair in VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY and VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY — the same pair everywhere (local .env and the Render environment). A browser subscribed with one public key cannot receive pushes signed with another, and changing the keys cuts off every existing subscription.
  3. In the app, turn on Settings → Reminders → Notify me on this device and allow notifications when the browser asks. If it was already on before the keys were set, turn it off and on again.

Push only works in a production build. The service worker that receives pushes is registered only when import.meta.env.PROD is true, so under npm run dev the app falls back to in-app notifications: they appear only while a logbook tab is open, and the tab checks for due reminders every five minutes. Test real push against the deployed site, with the logbook tab closed but the browser still running.

If notifications never appear, check in order: the browser's site permission for notifications (Notification.permission in the console should be "granted"), the operating system's notification settings for the browser (including Do Not Disturb), and — on the deployed site — that the backend is awake, since Render's free tier sleeps when idle and pushes are only sent while it runs. On iPhone, push requires the app to be added to the home screen. Notification sound is controlled by the operating system, not the app.

docs.text: The short version, for anyone adding a feature: a feature is not done until it has a test file, the suite is green, and coverage stays above 50%. The full story is on the Testing page.

  • Frontend → apps/frontend/src/**/__tests__/YourFeature.test.tsx — render the real component with React Testing Library (copy the structure of pages/__tests__/ProjectsPage.test.tsx).

Cover the happy path and the obvious failure path (invalid input, missing auth), and clean up any data the test creates.

From the repository root:

npm run test --workspace=apps/backend -- src/__tests__/yourFeature.test.ts
npm run test --workspace=apps/frontend -- src/pages/__tests__/YourFeature.test.tsx

# the full suite, before you push
npm run test --workspace=apps/backend
npm run test --workspace=apps/frontend

Run the suite with coverage:

npm run test:coverage --workspace=apps/backend
npm run test:coverage --workspace=apps/frontend

The end of the output is a table. Read the All files row — the last number is % Lines, the number coverage is measured on. Backend example, from the 2026-09-28 run:

File      | % Stmts | % Branch | % Funcs | % Lines
All files |   84.38 |    79.73 |   90.88 |   85.12

docs.title: 4. The 50% rule
docs.text:
The project must stay above 50% combined coverage — that is the figure the marking rubric reads. Where it stands (2026-09-28, 960 tests):

Workspace % Lines Backend 85.12% (1,843 of 2,165 lines) Frontend 59.54% (2,242 of 3,765 lines) Combined 68.89% (4,085 of 5,930 lines)

The margin over the bar is real but not free: the frontend is the lower of the two, so untested frontend code moves the combined figure most — test the code you add. After you push, CI runs both suites and publishes coverage/backend, coverage/frontend and coverage/combined on your commit in Gitea; a red run blocks the merge.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: This page documents how the Digital Logbook is tested: our test stack and why we chose it, what is covered by automated tests, the formal user feedback process, our testing policy, and proof of passing runs.

docs.title: Test Stack & Why We Chose It
docs.text:
Tool Role Why Vitest 4 Test runner and assertion framework Same engine that powers our frontend build tooling (Vite), so one dependency ecosystem covers the whole monorepo. Fast, ESM-native, and watch-mode works out of the box with TypeScript — no extra transpile config. Supertest HTTP-level request helper (backend) Lets tests call the Express app directly (request(app).post(...)) without starting a real server or opening a port. We test the real HTTP layer — routing, middleware, validation, status codes, JSON bodies — not just functions. React Testing Library Component testing (frontend) Tests components the way users interact with them — finding elements by placeholder text, role, and label rather than by implementation details like CSS class or component state. jsdom Browser environment for frontend tests Provides a lightweight DOM inside Node.js so React components can render, fire events, and validate forms without a real browser. The real Express app (src/app.ts) System under test (backend) The app module is exported separately from the server entry point (src/index.ts) precisely so tests can import it without binding port 3000. Live PostgreSQL (Neon) Real database (backend) Integration tests run against the actual database the app uses, exercising real Prisma queries, real constraints (unique, cascade deletes), and real SQL aggregation. Mocking Prisma would test our mocks, not our app. otplib TOTP code generation in tests The 2FA tests generate genuinely valid time-based codes with the same library the server uses to verify them, so the full TOTP round-trip is tested end-to-end.

Testing pyramid: the backend has integration tests (API-level, real database) and unit tests (pure functions); the frontend has component tests (rendered React components with jsdom) and unit tests (pure logic like saved-filter persistence).

docs.title: How the Tests Work
docs.text:
Backend API test — a real HTTP request to the real Express app backed by the real database:

it("PATCH /entries/:id/status marks entry DONE and sets completedAt", async () => {
  const res = await request(app)          // real Express app, no port
    .patch(`/api/entries/${statusEntryId}/status`)
    .set(H)                                // Authorization: Bearer <real JWT>
    .send({ status: "DONE" });

  expect(res.status).toBe(200);
  expect(res.body.status).toBe("DONE");
  expect(res.body.completedAt).not.toBeNull();
});

Frontend component test — renders the real React component in jsdom and asserts on DOM output:

it("renders the session-expired banner when the URL has ?expired=1", () => {
  window.history.pushState({}, "", "/login?expired=1");
  renderLoginPage();
  expect(screen.getByText(/session expired/i)).toBeInTheDocument();
});

Backend unit test — exercises pure functions directly:

it("verifyToken returns null for a tampered token", () => {
  const token = generateToken("user-1");
  const tampered = token.slice(0, -1) + (token.endsWith("A") ? "B" : "A");
  expect(verifyToken(tampered)).toBeNull();
});

Shared conventions across test files:

  • Own user per file (backend). Each suite creates its own test user (unique UUID + timestamped email), so suites never collide even though Vitest runs test files in parallel.
  • Setup in beforeAll, cleanup via cascade (backend). Fixed data is created once; afterAll deletes the test user and every foreign key is ON DELETE CASCADE.
  • Sequential within a suite where one test's output feeds the next (the 2FA lifecycle).
  • API modules mocked at the boundary (frontend). Frontend component tests mock ../api so they test the UI layer in isolation from the backend.
  • 15s per-test timeout for backend tests — the database is remote (Neon), so round-trips cost ~500ms each.

docs.title: How to Run Them
docs.text:
# Backend tests (from the repository root)
npm run test --workspace=apps/backend

# Frontend tests
npm run test --workspace=apps/frontend

# Watch mode (re-runs on file changes)
npm run test:watch --workspace=apps/backend
npm run test:watch --workspace=apps/frontend

Backend prerequisites: a reachable DATABASE_URL in apps/backend/.env and a regenerated Prisma client (npx prisma generate in apps/backend — see Bugs Found By Testing).

Email behaviour in tests: with no SMTP credentials configured, registration auto-verifies (dev mode) and password-reset emails fail silently — both are caught and logged, and the endpoints still behave correctly. The tests assert the HTTP contract, never the email delivery.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
Coverage is measured with Vitest's V8 provider, configured in apps/backend/vitest.config.ts and in the test.coverage block of apps/frontend/vite.config.ts.

# Backend coverage (needs the same DATABASE_URL as the ordinary run)
npm run test:coverage --workspace=apps/backend

# Frontend coverage
npm run test:coverage --workspace=apps/frontend

Each run prints a summary table to the terminal and writes lcov.info to <workspace>/coverage/, which most editors and coverage viewers read directly. The coverage/ directories are gitignored; the numbers belong in CI output and in this document, not in the repository.

Both suites are configured with include: ["src/**"]. Vitest 4 removed the older coverage.all option, and without naming the sources explicitly a file that no test touches is simply absent from the report rather than counted as zero. Listing them keeps the percentage honest: it is coverage of the codebase, not coverage of the files that happen to have tests. Test files and the frontend's test-setup.ts and main.tsx are excluded, since measuring the tests against themselves says nothing.

docs.title: In CI
docs.text:
.gitea/workflows/deploy.yaml runs test:coverage rather than test for both workspaces on every push to main, master, Alondwe and Dineo. The text reporter puts the coverage table directly into the Actions log, so the numbers can be read from a run without downloading anything, and the two lcov.info files are uploaded as a coverage-lcov artifact.

The upload step is pinned to actions/upload-artifact@v3 and marked continue-on-error. Version 4 of that action depends on an artifact backend that not every Gitea runner provides, and a runner without artifact storage should not fail an otherwise green build — the coverage table is in the log regardless.

docs.title: Coverage on the commit
docs.text:
Gitea 1.24 has no built-in coverage display of the kind GitLab offers, so the workflow publishes the figure itself. .gitea/scripts/report-coverage.mjs reads the coverage-summary.json each workspace writes and posts three commit statuses through the Gitea API: coverage/backend, coverage/frontend and coverage/combined, each described as a line percentage and linking back to the run that produced it. They appear on the commit in the Gitea UI, so the number is visible per commit with no manual step.

The combined status is the one the marking rubric is judged on, which is why it is published rather than left for a reader to work out from the other two.

The script is Node rather than shell because jq and curl are not guaranteed on a self-hosted runner while Node is, setup-node having already run. It never fails the build: a missing summary, a missing token, a rejected request and an unreachable host are all logged and exited cleanly, and the step is additionally marked continue-on-error. Publishing a number is not worth turning a green run red.

It also appends the same table to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY, which renders on the run page for runners that support summaries and is ignored by those that do not.

If the statuses do not appear, the log will say why — the likeliest cause is the runner's injected token lacking permission to write statuses, in which case a repository secret holding a token with write access can be passed to the step instead.

No coverage thresholds are enforced yet. The purpose at this stage is to publish the numbers and watch them move; a threshold set before anyone has seen a baseline is an arbitrary number that either passes trivially or blocks work for no reason. Once a few runs have established where the project actually sits, a floor at or slightly below the current figure is worth adding, so coverage can only go up.

docs.title: The CI database link, and the ETIMEDOUT failures
docs.text:
The backend suites run against the hosted Neon database over the public internet. CI has failed repeatedly with ETIMEDOUT — a transport error, raised before the statement ever reached Postgres — landing on an arbitrary query while everything around it read and wrote to the same database without trouble.

This section has now been wrong twice, so it records what was ruled out as carefully as what was tried.

Ruled out by measurement. Capping the worker count cut peak concurrency threefold and the failure did not move, which rules out connection-pool pressure. Other suites complete writes seconds before a failure in the same run, which rules out a cold start of the serverless compute.

Tried and did not work. The pool was created with a connection string and nothing else, so every pg.Pool default applied, including keepAlive: false. Enabling keepalive looked like the answer — DATABASE_URL points at Neon's -pooler endpoint, which drops connections that go quiet. It did not fix it: the next run went from three failures to eight. keepAlive is kept because it is right for a long-lived pool against a pooler, but it is not the cause. A speculative max: 5 added at the same time was removed again; it had no evidence behind it and the run got slower.

What the evidence actually showed. In the run of 2026-09-27 every one of the eight failures was a read that timed out: four in loadHistory's findFirst, three in the findUniqueOrThrow that takes the pre-edit snapshot in updateEntry, one in getEntries' findMany. Several surfaced not as an error but as a wrong answer downstream — an entry stuck at version 1, a time summary reading 30 instead of 90 — because the read failed inside a handler that carried on regardless.

The fix that follows from that. utils/readRetry.ts retries an operation only when both hold: it is one of the eight idempotent reads, and it failed with a transport code (ETIMEDOUT, ECONNRESET, ECONNREFUSED, EPIPE, or Prisma's P1001, P1002, P1017). Up to three attempts, with a growing pause. It is applied to every query through a Prisma client extension in prisma.ts.

Three things it deliberately never does: retry a write, because one that timed out at the transport may still have landed; retry raw SQL, because $queryRawUnsafe could be anything; and retry an error the database actually returned, so a constraint violation is still raised on the first attempt and cannot be hidden. readRetry.test.ts holds each of those as its own test.

This is also right beyond CI. A student should not see a 500 because one TCP connection went quiet between two of their queries, and a question asked twice returns the same answer.

The retry in entriesListing.test.ts predates this and is kept; its setup writes are idempotent by construction, since the user fixture upserts and the entry seed is guarded by a row count.

If ETIMEDOUT still reaches an assertion after this, the next thing to examine is load rather than connections: the suite runs for eight minutes against a free-tier instance, and automationEngine alone accounts for six of those.

docs.title: Testing Policy
docs.text:
1. Every API endpoint gets tests for the happy path and its error paths (400 validation, 401 auth, 404 missing, 409 conflict). If an endpoint has no error-path test, it isn't done.
  2. Never mock what we're testing at the integration level. No Prisma mocks, no stub auth. The database is real; failures must be real failures. Unit tests for pure functions may use mocks for external dependencies.
  3. Security behaviour is tested as behaviour, not implementation — e.g. we assert that unknown-email and wrong-password logins return byte-identical errors, not that some flag was set.
  4. Tests must clean up after themselves via user-cascade deletion, so the shared database stays usable.
  5. Regression rule: any bug found (see below) gets a test that would have caught it before the fix is considered done.
  6. Tests run in CI before every merge to main — a red suite blocks the merge. The Gitea Actions workflow runs both backend and frontend test suites on every push to protected branches.

docs.title: User Feedback Process
docs.text:
Automated testing checks what the code does; user feedback checks whether it works for real users. Our formal process:

  1. Instrument: a standard SUS (System Usability Scale) questionnaire — 10 fixed Likert items, scored 0–100 — so results are quantifiable and comparable across rounds.
  2. Scenario-based sessions: each tester gets the same set of task scenarios (register → create project → add entry → mark done → view stats/calendar → enable 2FA). We record pass/fail per task and where testers hesitate.
  3. Recruitment: 5–8 testers per round — classmates, other teams, and our client.
  4. Analysis & integration: SUS scores and task failures are reviewed as a team; each actionable finding becomes an issue on the tracker with an assigned fix, and fixed items are reported back in the next round.
  5. Records: each round is logged in docs/user-feedback.md with the raw scores, findings, and the feedback → action → commit trail.

The first formal round is scheduled for Sprint 2; results will be published on this site.

docs.title: Proof of Passing Runs
docs.text: Run date: 2026-09-28 · 960 / 960 tests passing · 57 / 57 test files passing

docs.title: Bugs Found By Testing
docs.text:
Writing these tests surfaced two real issues — this is the regression rule in action:

  1. Stale Prisma client broke every entry-creation test (11 pre-existing failures). The generated client predated the Sprint 2 schema, so any query touching entry_fields.archived_at threw PrismaClientValidationError: Unknown argument archivedAt. Fix: run npx prisma generate after pulling schema changes. Lesson: prisma generate belongs in postinstall/CI.

  2. Concurrent entry-field creation can race on format versioning. Each field create does read-latest-version → insert latest+1. Two parallel creates both read version N and both try to insert N+1; the unique (project_id, version) constraint rejects one, so one field creation fails with 400. Fixed (BUG-001): the version bump now runs in a transaction and retries on a unique-constraint collision, so the loser of the race reads again and takes the next number. entryFieldIntegrity.test.ts creates and deletes fields concurrently and checks every version number is distinct and gapless.

docs.title: Third-Party Code
docs.text:
This page documents every third-party library and external service the Digital Logbook depends on, and — more importantly — why each one was chosen. Our policy is to lean on well-maintained, permissively licensed libraries for solved problems (authentication primitives, email, build tooling) while hand-writing everything that is core to the product (the REST API, business logic, database schema and UI components).

Every package below is declared in package.json (per workspace) and its license was verified from the installed package.json on disk.

docs.title: How we evaluate dependencies
docs.text:
Before adding a library we check:

  1. Fit — does it solve a problem we would otherwise hand-roll poorly (crypto, date handling, bundling)?
  2. Maintenance — is it actively maintained and widely adopted?
  3. License — permissive (MIT / BSD / Apache-2.0) so it is safe for a university project; no copyleft surprises.
  4. Size — is the dependency worth its footprint on the bundle?

docs.title: Backend runtime dependencies
docs.text: Package License What it does Why we chose it express ^5.2 MIT HTTP framework for the REST API Minimal and unopinionated — the course requires a hand-written API, and Express gives us routing/middleware without generating code or hiding the API behind heavy abstractions. v5 has native async error handling. @prisma/client ^7.9 Apache-2.0 Type-safe database access The generated client turns every query into TypeScript-checked code — schema drift becomes a compile error, not a runtime crash. Schema-as-code also gives us reviewable migrations. @prisma/adapter-pg ^7.9 Apache-2.0 Driver adapter for PostgreSQL Prisma's driver-adapter pattern lets us bring our own pg connection pool, which is the recommended way to talk to Neon's serverless Postgres over a pooled connection string. pg ^8.23 MIT PostgreSQL wire-protocol driver Required by the Prisma adapter; a mature, battle-tested driver. zod ^4.4 MIT Schema validation One validation library shared by frontend and backend through @logbook/shared — the same Zod schema validates the register form in React and the request body on the server. Single source of truth, no drift. jsonwebtoken ^9.0 MIT Signs and verifies JWTs Stateless auth: the server issues a signed token and verifies it on every request without a session store. The de-facto standard library for HS256 JWTs in Node. bcryptjs ^3.0 BSD-3-Clause Password hashing Pure-JavaScript bcrypt. We chose it over the native bcrypt package specifically because it needs no compilation — no node-gyp/native-module issues on teammates' Windows laptops. Same algorithm, identical hashes. otplib ^13.5 MIT TOTP two-factor authentication (RFC 6238) Implements the same standard that Google Authenticator / Authy use, so users can use any authenticator app. Actively maintained successor to speakeasy. qrcode ^1.5 MIT QR code generation Renders the otpauth:// provisioning URI as a QR data URL so users can scan it with their phone camera instead of typing a base32 secret. nodemailer ^9.0 MIT-0 Transactional email over SMTP Works with any SMTP provider — we send through Gmail with an app password — so there is no vendor lock-in and it works in local development without an API account. cors ^2.8 MIT Cross-Origin Resource Sharing middleware The frontend (Vite dev server on :5173, deployed frontend on Cloudflare Pages) calls the backend on a different origin; cors handles the preflight/OPTIONS dance correctly. dotenv ^17.4 BSD-2-Clause Loads .env into process.env Twelve-factor configuration: secrets (DB URL, JWT secret, Gmail credentials) stay out of the codebase. resend ^6.20 MIT Email API client Preferred email provider when RESEND_API_KEY is set; Gmail SMTP is the fallback. A REST API avoids SMTP ports that some hosts block. web-push ^3.6 MPL-2.0 Sends reminder push notifications Implements the standard Web Push protocol with VAPID keys, so the server can notify a student's devices directly through each browser's own push service — no third-party notification account or per-message cost. express-rate-limit ^8.7 MIT Rate limiting on the auth routes Caps sign-in, sign-up and 2FA attempts per IP to slow down password and code guessing (BUG-003). A small, standard Express middleware rather than a hand-rolled counter. googleapis ^181 Apache-2.0 Google Calendar API client and OAuth 2.0 Our external API integration: syncs entry due dates into the user's Google Calendar. Google's official client handles the OAuth code exchange and refreshes access tokens automatically.

docs.title: Licensing summary
docs.text: All dependencies use permissive licenses — MIT, BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause, ISC, Apache-2.0 or MIT-0 — with one exception: web-push is under the Mozilla Public License 2.0. MPL-2.0 is a weak, file-level copyleft: it applies only to changes made to web-push's own files, which we use unmodified from npm. It places no obligations on our code, so the project's own licensing is unaffected. There is no GPL or AGPL code in the dependency tree.

docs.title: User Feedback
docs.text: This page documents the formal user feedback process we use to improve the Digital Logbook. Feedback is collected through a standardised instrument — the System Usability Scale (SUS) — combined with task-scenario observations and open-ended responses. Findings are tracked and every actionable change is recorded in the integration table at the bottom of this page.

docs.title: Why we collect feedback
docs.text: Automated tests verify that the code does what we intend; user feedback verifies that the product works for the people it's for. The feedback process is a required part of our methodology: every round of collection is followed by a round of integration, where each actionable finding becomes a tracked issue with an assigned fix.

docs.title: The formal process
docs.text: Stage What happens Instrument A Google Form with the 10 standard SUS items, 7 task-completion self-reports, and open-ended questions. Testers 5–8 per round: classmates, members of other teams, and our client (where available). Demographics are captured in the form itself. Session format 15–20 minutes, supervised. The tester works through the 7 task scenarios on the live app while an observer notes pass/fail and friction points on the observation sheet below. Recording Form responses land in a linked Google Sheet. An observer's written notes are kept alongside as a second data source. Analysis SUS scores per tester (0–100) and an average across the round; per-task pass/fail counts; open-ended responses grouped by theme. Integration Every actionable finding becomes an issue on the bug tracker with an owner and a fix commit. The integration table below records the full trail.

docs.title: The feedback form
docs.text:
Link: https://forms.gle/g4gEzYtiFRSXCQ5CA

The form is structured in four sections:

  1. Welcome & About You — consent statement, role (Student / Lecturer or tutor / Working professional / Other), and prior experience with digital logbooks or work-tracking tools.
  2. Task Feedback — for each of 7 tasks (register, create project, add entry, mark done, view stats, view calendar/board, enable 2FA), the tester self-reports Completed easily / Completed with some difficulty / Could not complete, plus an optional comment field per task.
  3. System Usability Scale — the 10 standard SUS items on a 5-point Likert scale (Strongly disagree → Strongly agree). Worded verbatim; the SUS instrument is free to use and publicly cited across HCI research.
  4. Open Feedback — most frustrating part (required), favourite feature, one-thing-to-change, and an NPS-style 0–10 recommend-likelihood scale.

A screenshot of the published form is captured after each round. The raw response data for each round is stored as a CSV file in this repository (e.g. docs/user-feedback-round1.csv).

docs.title: Observation sheet (for the supervisor)
docs.text:
Self-reported answers are one half of the evidence; the other half is what the observer actually sees. For each session, fill in this table on paper alongside the tester:

Task Completed Notes / friction points 1. Register a new account ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ 2. Log in and create a project with custom fields ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ 3. Add a logbook entry (with duration + due date) ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ 4. Mark an entry as done ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ 5. Check project statistics (totals, averages) ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ 6. Find calendar and board views ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ 7. Enable two-factor authentication ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌

✅ = completed easily · ⚠️ = completed with difficulty · ❌ = could not complete.

docs.title: SUS scoring (in the linked Google Sheet)
docs.text:
When the form is linked to a Google Sheet (Responses → create spreadsheet), add these helper columns to auto-score each row:

Column Header Formula SUS_1 q1_adj =B2-1 (odd item: subtract 1) SUS_2 q2_adj =5-C2 (even item: 5 − answer) SUS_3 q3_adj =D2-1 SUS_4 q4_adj =5-E2 SUS_5 q5_adj =F2-1 SUS_6 q6_adj =5-G2 SUS_7 q7_adj =H2-1 SUS_8 q8_adj =5-I2 SUS_9 q9_adj =J2-1 SUS_10 q10_adj =5-K2 SUS score =SUM(q1_adj:q10_adj) * 2.5 (yields 0–100)

Adjust column letters to match the actual sheet columns produced by the grid question. The pattern — odd items score answer − 1, even items score 5 − answer, then sum and multiply by 2.5 — is the canonical SUS calculation from Brooke (1996).

Average SUS across the round: =AVERAGE(SUS_score_range). Industry benchmarks (Sauro, 2011) place the average SUS at 68/100; anything above ~72 is above-average, above ~80 is excellent.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Digital Logbook is designed as a non-monolithic web application consisting of a React frontend, an Express backend, and a PostgreSQL database.

The frontend communicates with the backend through a hand-written REST API. The backend handles business logic, authentication, validation, and database access.

This page explains the design decisions. For the system as built (deployment, folder layout, data model, API areas and background jobs), see System Architecture.

docs.title: Separation of Concerns
docs.text:
Layer Responsibility Technology Presentation UI rendering, user interaction, client-side routing, offline cache React 19, Tailwind CSS v4 API Request handling, authentication, validation, business logic Express 5, Zod, JWT Background work Recurring entries, reminder pushes, account purges Jobs in the API process Data Access Type-safe database queries, migrations Prisma ORM 7 Persistence Relational data storage PostgreSQL (Neon) Shared Common types and validation schemas @logbook/shared

The frontend never accesses the database directly. All data flows through the backend API, ensuring consistent validation and authentication enforcement.

docs.title: Authentication Flow
docs.text:
┌──────────┐    POST /api/auth/login        ┌──────────┐
│  Client  │  ───────────────────────────►  │ Backend  │
│  (React) │     email + password           │  bcrypt  │
│          │                                │  verify  │
│          │  ◄───────────────────────────  │          │
│          │  JWT, or "2FA required" +      │          │
│          │  5-minute pending token        │          │
│          │                                │          │
│          │    POST /api/auth/login/2fa    │  TOTP or │
│          │  ───────────────────────────►  │ recovery │
│          │  pending token + code          │  code    │
│          │  ◄───────────────────────────  │          │
│          │    JWT (7 days)                │          │
│          │                                │          │
│  Attach  │    GET /api/projects           │ require- │
│  token   │  ───────────────────────────►  │ Auth     │
│          │  ◄───────────────────────────  │          │
│          │    the user's own data         │          │
└──────────┘                                └──────────┘
  1. The user registers with email and password; the password is hashed with bcrypt before storage.
  2. A verification email is sent through Resend or Gmail SMTP. With no email provider configured (development), the account is verified automatically. Sign-in is refused until the email is verified.
  3. On sign-in, the password is checked. Without 2FA, a signed JWT valid for seven days is returned.
  4. With 2FA on, the backend instead returns a pending token that is valid for five minutes and good only for the second step. The client sends it with a code from the authenticator app, or a single-use recovery code, and receives the JWT. A code on its own is never enough to sign in.
  5. The frontend stores the JWT in localStorage and attaches it to every request through an Axios interceptor.
  6. The backend requireAuth middleware validates the token on protected routes.
  7. When a protected request returns 401 (the token expired or is invalid), the frontend clears the session and returns to /login?expired=1. A wrong password on a credential check is not treated as an expired session.

docs.title: Request Processing Pipeline
docs.text:
Every API request flows through the following pipeline:

Request → CORS → Body Parser → Rate Limit → Auth Middleware → Zod Validation → Ownership Check → Controller → Prisma → Response
  1. CORS: allows requests only from the frontend origins (localhost and *.pages.dev).
  2. Body Parser: parses JSON request bodies.
  3. Rate Limit: applies to /api/auth routes, with tighter limits on sign-in, sign-up and 2FA, to slow down password guessing.
  4. Auth Middleware: verifies the JWT and sets the user id (skipped for public routes).
  5. Zod Validation: validates the request body against its schema (400 on failure).
  6. Ownership Check: loads the project, entry, rule or statistic named in the path only if it belongs to the signed-in user. A resource owned by someone else is reported as not found (404), so its existence is not revealed.
  7. Controller: executes business logic.
  8. Prisma: performs type-safe database operations, in a transaction where several rows must change together.
  9. Response: returns JSON with the appropriate status code.

A valid token only proves who the caller is, not what they may touch, so the ownership check is a separate step on every route that names a resource.

docs.title: Shared Types
docs.text: Types and validation schemas that both sides need live in one package, @logbook/shared, so the frontend and backend cannot disagree about data shapes. The frontend reads the package's source directly. The backend uses its compiled output, so the package must be rebuilt after a change before the backend sees it. See System Architecture.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Digital Logbook uses a PostgreSQL database to store users, projects, project entry formats, logbook entries and their history, and the features built on top of them: tags, statistics, dashboards, automation and reminders.

A key design goal was that different projects need different logbook entry structures (e.g. one project may track "hours worked" and "task completed", while another tracks "description" and "outcome"). Rather than hardcoding a fixed set of columns for logbook entries, we adopted an Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV) pattern using ENTRY_FIELD and ENTRY_VALUE. This trades some query simplicity for the flexibility of letting each project define its own entry format without requiring schema changes.

We use UUIDs rather than auto-incrementing integers as primary keys to avoid exposing sequential, guessable IDs and to make it easier to merge or migrate data across environments without ID collisions.
